¶
{{smaller block|He came down with a huge long naked weapon in both his hands, and looked so dreadfully! sure he’s ''beside himself.''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 2.}}}}
'''To go beside†''', to pass by; pass over.—'''To look beside†''', to overlook; fail to see; miss seeing.
{{smaller block|Let vs but open our eyes, we cannot ''looke beside'' a lesson.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'' (1627), Epistles, iv. 341.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Beside, Besides. Beside'', by the side of; ''besides'', in addition to.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then went Sir Bedivere the second time
Across the ridge, and paced ''beside'' the mere.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.}}
His [Muley Abul Hassan’s] kingdom now contained fourteen cities, ninety-seven fortified places, ''besides'' numerous unwalled towns and villages defended by formidable castles.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 13.}}}}

'''besidery†''' (bẹ̄-sī′de-ri), ''n.'' [Origin unknown.] A species of pear. ''Johnson.''

'''besides''' (bẹ̄-sīdz′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'' [< ME. ''besides, bisides'', < ''beside'' + adv. gen. suffix ''-es'': see ''beside''.] '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Moreover; more than that; further.
{{smaller block|<poem>The match
Were rich and honourable; ''besides'', the gentleman
Is full of virtue, bounty, worth, and qualities
Beseeming such a wife as your fair daughter.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' In addition; over and above; as well.
{{smaller block|The men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any ''besides?''
{{right|Gen. xix. 12.}}
There are ''besides'' many pompous volumes, some emboss’d with gold, and intaglias on achats, medailes, etc.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Sept. 2, 1680.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>Flutter’d in the ''besieging'' wind’s uproar,
And the long carpets rose along the gusty floor.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Eve of St. Agnes, xl.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' To beset, hem in, invest, blockade.

'''besieged''' (bē-sējd′), ''p. a.'' In ''astrol.'', said of a planet which is between two others.

'''besiegement''' (bē-sēj′ment), ''n.'' [< ''besiege'' + ''-ment.''] '''1.''' The act of besieging.—'''2.''' A state of siege; beleaguerment.
{{smaller block|It is not probable, however, that Pemberton would have permitted a close ''besiegement.''
{{right|''U. S. Grant'', Personal Memoirs, I. 495.}}}}

'''besieger''' (bē-sē′jėr), ''n.'' One who besieges.
{{smaller block|On the 27th of November, the ''besiegers'' made a desperate though ineffectual assault on the city.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 23.}}}}

'''besieging''' (bē-sē′jing), ''p. a.'' Surrounding in a hostile manner; employed in a siege: as, a ''besieging'' army.

'''besiegingly''' (bē-sē′jing-li), ''adv.'' In a besieging manner. [Rare.]

'''besilver''' (bē-sil′vėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''silver.''] To cover with or as with silver. ''G. Fletcher.''

'''besing''' (bē-sing′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''sing.''] To sing about; celebrate in song. ''Carlyle.''

'''besit†''' (bē-sit′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''besitten'', < AS. ''besittan'', sit about, < ''be-'', about, + ''sittan'', sit: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''sit'', and cf. the causal form ''beset.''] '''1.''' To sit about; besiege.—'''2.''' To sit upon.—'''3.''' To sit properly upon, as clothes; suit; become.
{{smaller block|{{c|That which is for Ladies most ''besitting.''}}
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. ii. 19.}}}}

'''beslave''' (bē-slāv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''slave''.] To make a slave of; enslave.
{{smaller block|[Covetousness] ''beslaves'' the affections.
{{right|''Quarles'', Judgment and Mercy.}}}}

'''beslaver''' (bẹ̄-slav′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''slaver''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''beslabber''.] To cover with slaver, or anything suggesting slaver; hence, to cover with fulsome flattery.

'''beslik''' (bes′lik), ''n.'' Same as ''beshlik''.

'''beslime''' (bẹ̄-slīm′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''slime''.] To daub with or as with slime; soil.
{{smaller block|Our fry of writers may ''beslime'' his fame.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Prol. to Poetaster.}}}}

'''beslobber''' (bẹ̄-slob′ėr), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''besloberen'', same as ''beslaberen'': see ''beslabber''.] To besmear or befoul with spittle or anything running from the mouth; slobber over with effusive kisses; hence, to flatter in a fulsome manner or to a fulsome degree.

{{smaller block|''Beslubber'' our garments with it [blood].
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|beset|532|besmear}}</noinclude>''set.''] '''1†.''' To set or place.—'''2.''' To set or place upon; distribute over; bestud; besprinkle: now only in the perfect participle.
{{smaller block|The garden is so ''beset'' with all manner of sweete shrubbs, that it perfumes the aire. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 22, 1685.}}}}
{{smaller block|A robe of azure ''beset'' with drops of gold.
{{right|''Spectator'', No. 425.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Beset'' on its external surface with spines.
{{right|''W. B. Carpenter'', Micros., § 532.}}}}
'''3.''' To come upon or against; set upon in attack, or so as to perplex, endanger, or hem in; press upon severely, vigorously, or from all sides: as, to ''beset'' one with blows or with entreaties.
{{smaller block|Let us lay aside . . . the sin which doth so easily ''beset'' us.
{{right|Heb. xii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|We are ''beset'' with thieves. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Adam sore ''beset'' replied. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 124.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let thy troops ''beset'' our gates. {{right|''Addison'', Cato.}}}}
{{smaller block|We had been ''beset'' [with ice] fifteen days, and had drifted twenty-two miles to the southward.
{{right|''A. W. Greely'', Arctic Service, xxxviii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The main difficulty ''besetting'' the theory of the excavation of the rock basins by ice is to explain how the ice after entering the basin manages to get out again.
{{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Cosmology, p. 254.}}}}
'''4†.''' To employ; spend; use up.   ''Chaucer.''—'''5†.''' To become; suit; look well on.—'''To be beset on†''', {{smaller|to be occupied with; have one’s mind fixed on.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>God wolde,
Syn thou most love thurgh thy destenee
That thou ''beset were on'' swich on that sholde
Know al thi wo, al lakkede here pitee.</poem> {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 521.}}}}

'''besetment''' (bē-set′ment), ''n.''   [< ''beset'' + ''-ment.'']   '''1.''' The state or condition of being beset.
{{smaller block|The breeze freshened off shore, breaking up and sending out the floes, the leads rapidly closing. Fearing a ''besetment'', I determined to fasten to an iceberg.
{{right|''Kane'', Sec. Grinn. Exp., I. 33.}}}}
'''2.''' The sin or failing to which one is most liable; a besetting sin or tendency. [From the expression in Heb. xii. 1.]
{{smaller block|It’s my ''besetment'' to forget where I am, and everything around me. {{right|''George Eliot.''}}}}

'''besetting''' (bē-set′ing), ''p. a.'' Habitually attacking or waylaying.
{{smaller block|We have all of us our ''besetting'' sins, our special moral danger, and our special moral strength.
{{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, ix.}}}}

'''besew†''' (bē-sō′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''besewen'', < ''be-'' + ''sewen'', sew: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''sew''<sup>1</sup>.]   To sew.   ''Gower.''

'''beseye†''', ''pp.'' A Middle English form of ''beseen.''

'''besha''' (bē′shä̤), ''n.'' An ancient Egyptian measure of capacity, said to be equal to 4.5 liters, or one imperial gallon.

'''beshet†''', ''pp.'' A past participle of ''beshut.''   ''Chaucer.''

'''beshine†''' (bē-shīn′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''beshone'', ppr. ''beshining.''   [< ME. ''beshinen'', ''bischinen'', < AS. ''bescīnan'' (= OFries. ''bischīna'' = D. ''beschijnen'' = OHG. ''bisceinan'', MHG. ''beschinen'', G. ''bescheinen'' = Goth. ''biskeinan''), shine upon, < ''be-'' + ''scīnan'', shine: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''shine.'']   To shine about or upon.   ''Chaucer.''
{{smaller block|[She] was as fair a creature as the sun might ''beshine.''
{{right|''Beryn'', l. 381.}}}}

'''beshlik''' (besh′lik), ''n.'' A Turkish silver coin, of the value of 21 United States cents. Also ''beslik.''

'''beshmet''' (besh′met), ''n.''   [Native term.]   An article of food consisting of grapes made into the consistence of honey, used among the tribes of the mountainous districts of Asia Minor.

'''beshone†''' (bẹ̄-shōn′). Preterit and past participle of ''beshine.''

'''beshow''' (bẹ̄-shō′), ''n.'' A name given by the Indians of the strait of Juan de Fuca to the candle-fish, ''Anoplopoma fimbria.'' See cut under ''candle-fish.''

'''beshrew''' (bẹ̄-shrö′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beshrewen,'' curse, pervert, < ''be-'' + ''shrew'': see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''shrew''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' To wish a curse to; execrate.
{{smaller block|Alle suche freendis I ''beshrewe.''
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>See, a blossom from the bough;
But ''beshrew'' his heart that pull’d it.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Nay, quoth the cock; but I ''beshrew'' us both,
If I believe a saint upon his oath.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Cock and Fox.}}}}

'''2.''' In modern use, a mildly imprecatory or merely expletive introductory exclamation, in the form of the imperative.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Beshrew'' your heart,
Fair daughter! you do draw my spirits from me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Beshrew'' me, but it was an absolute good jest.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Beshrew'' the sombre pencil! said I vauntingly.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey.}}}}
<poem>It was an idle bolt I sent, against the villain crow;
Fair sir, I fear it harmed thy hand; ''beshrew'' my erring bow!</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Bryant'', Strange Lady.}}}}

'''beshroud''' (bē-shroud′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''shroud.'']   To cover with or as with a shroud; hide in darkness, as with a cloak.

'''beshut†''' (bē̤-shut′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''beshutten'', ''bishetten'', < ''be-'' + ''shutten'', shut: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''shut.'']   To shut in or inclose; shut up or confine.

'''besiclometer''' (bes-i-klom′e-tėr), ''n.''   [< F. ''besicles'', spectacles (modified (as if < ''bes'', L. ''bis'', twice, + L. ''oculus'', eye) < OF. ''bericle'', crystal, spectacles, dim. < L. ''beryllus'': see ''beryl'' and ''brills''), + Gr. μέτρον, a measure.]   An instrument for measuring the distance between the hinges of a pair of spectacles; a forehead-measure.

'''beside''' (bē-sīd′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.'', prop. ''prep. phr.''   [< ME. ''beside'', ''biside'', ''byside'', ''besiden'', ''bisiden'', etc., also (with adv. gen. suffix ''-es'') ''besides'', ''bisides'', adv. and prep., < AS. ''be sīdan'' (= MHG. ''besīten'', ''besīte''), by (the) side: ''be'', prep., E. ''by''; ''sīdan'', dat. of ''sīde'', side.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' Same as ''besides'', which is now the common form.

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' At the side of; near: as, sit down ''beside'' me, or ''beside'' the stream.
{{smaller block|''Beside'' him hung his bow. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 763.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I walking to and fro ''beside'' a stream.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}
'''2.''' Over and above; distinct from. [In this sense now rare, ''besides'' being used instead.]
{{smaller block|A woollen shirt is generally the only article of dress worn by the monks, ''beside'' the turban.
{{right|''E. W. Lane'', Modern Egyptians, II. 316.}}}}

'''3†.''' Out of; away from.
{{smaller block|One of them taking displeasure with his father . . . stepped to him, and plucking her [a falcon] ''beside'' [out of] his fist, wrong her neck.
{{right|''Holinshed'', Chron., Scotland (ed. 1806), II. 60.}}}}
{{smaller block|Neleus, Son of Codrus, being put ''beside'' [out of] the Kingdom of Athens by his younger Brother Medon.
{{right|''Stanley'', Hist. Philos. (ed. 1701). (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''4.''' Apart from; not connected with; not according to.
{{smaller block|It is ''beside'' my present business to enlarge upon this speculation.
{{right|''Locke.''}}}}

'''5†.''' Contrary to.
{{smaller block|At Durham, ''beside'' all expectation, I met an old friend.
{{right|''Johnson'', Letters (ed. 1788), I. lxxiii. 106.}}}}

'''6.''' Out of; in a state deviating from.
{{smaller block|<poem>Enough
To put him quite ''beside'' his patience.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 1.}}}}

'''7†.''' Without.
{{smaller block|<poem>Execut was al ''byside'' hire leve.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 622.}}}}

'''Beside the mark''', away from the mark aimed at; not to the point; irrelevant or irrelevantly: as, to shoot or to argue ''beside the mark.''
{{smaller block|To reason with such a writer is like talking to a deaf man who catches at a stray word, makes answer ''beside the mark'', and is led further and further into error by every attempt to explain.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Utilitarian Theory of Government.}}}}

'''To be beside one’s self''', to be out of one’s wits or senses; be in a high state of mental exaltation or excitement; lose one’s self-command through strong feeling.
{{smaller block|Paul, thou art ''beside thyself;'' much learning doth make thee mad.
{{right|Acts xxvi. 24.}}}}

{{smaller block|He came down with a huge long naked weapon in both his hands, and looked so dreadfully! sure he’s ''beside himself.''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epicœne, iv. 2.}}}}
'''To go beside†''', to pass by; pass over.—'''To look beside†''', to overlook; fail to see; miss seeing.
{{smaller block|Let vs but open our eyes, we cannot ''looke beside'' a lesson.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'' (1627), Epistles, iv. 341.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Beside, Besides. Beside'', by the side of; ''besides'', in addition to.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then went Sir Bedivere the second time
Across the ridge, and paced ''beside'' the mere.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Passing of Arthur.}}}}
{{smaller block|His [Muley Abul Hassan’s] kingdom now contained fourteen cities, ninety-seven fortified places, ''besides'' numerous unwalled towns and villages defended by formidable castles.
{{right|''Irving'', Granada, p. 13.}}}}

'''besidery†''' (bẹ̄-sī′de-ri), ''n.''   [Origin unknown.]   A species of pear.   ''Johnson.''

'''besides''' (bẹ̄-sīdz′), ''adv.'' and ''prep.''   [< ME. ''besides, bisides'', < ''beside'' + adv. gen. suffix ''-es'': see ''beside''.]   '''I.''' ''adv.'' '''1.''' Moreover; more than that; further.
{{smaller block|<poem>The match
Were rich and honourable; ''besides'', the gentleman
Is full of virtue, bounty, worth, and qualities
Beseeming such a wife as your fair daughter.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' In addition; over and above; as well.
{{smaller block|The men said unto Lot, Hast thou here any ''besides?''
{{right|Gen. xix. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|There are ''besides'' many pompous volumes, some emboss’d with gold, and intaglias on achats, medailes, etc.
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Sept. 2, 1680.}}}} '''3.''' Not included in that mentioned; otherwise; else.
{{smaller block|<poem>She does write to me
As if her heart were mines of adamant
To all the world ''besides.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, iii. 1.}}}}
'''4†.''' On one side; aside.
{{smaller block|<poem>To gon ''besydes'' in the weye.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 405.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou canst not fight: the blows thou mak’st at me
Are quite ''besides.'' ''Beau. and Fl.'', Maid’s Tragedy, v. 4.</poem>}}
Sometimes ''beside.''

'''II.''' ''prep.'' '''1†.''' By the side of; near.   ''Spenser.''—'''2.''' Over and above; separate or distinct from; in addition to: as, ''besides'' these honors he received much money.—'''3.''' Other than; except; bating.
{{smaller block|No living creature ever walks in it ''besides'' the chaplain.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 110.}}}}
'''4†.''' Beyond; away from: as, quite ''besides'' the subject.—{{smaller|'''Besides himself†''', beside himself. ''Holland'', tr. of Livy, p. 456.='''Syn.''' ''Beside, Besides.'' See ''beside'', II.}}

'''besiege''' (bē-sēj′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''besieged'', ppr. ''besieging''.   [< ME. ''besegen'', ''bisegen'', < ''be-'' + ''segen'', besiege: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''siege'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' To lay siege to; beleaguer; beset or surround with armed forces for the purpose of compelling to surrender, either by famine or by violent attacks: as, to ''besiege'' a castle or city.
{{smaller block|<poem>Till Paris was ''besieg’d'', famish’d, and lost.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To beset; throng around; harass.
{{smaller block|<poem>All frailties that ''besiege'' all kinds of blood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cix.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The arras, rich with horseman, hawk, and hound,</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Flutter’d in the ''besieging'' wind’s uproar,
And the long carpets rose along the gusty floor.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Eve of St. Agnes, xl.}}}}
